I kept the full divisor sum from my earlier answer, since "sum of the divisors" most commonly means σ(n), which includes n itself. The shared note offers proper divisors (excluding n) as an alternative. Switching would only require changing the starting value and skipping `n` in the loop.

```python
def sum_divisors(n):
    """Return the sum of all positive divisors of n (n >= 1), including n itself."""
    total = 0
    i = 1
    while i * i <= n:
        if n % i == 0:
            total += i
            j = n // i
            if j != i:
                total += j
        i += 1
    return total


def are_equivalent(a, b):
    """Return True if a and b have the same sum of divisors."""
    return sum_divisors(a) == sum_divisors(b)


assert are_equivalent(36, 57) == False
```

I checked the assert by hand: the divisors of 36 sum to 91 and those of 57 sum to 80, so the result is False. Under the proper-divisor reading the values are 55 and 23, which also gives False, so the assert does not tell the two interpretations apart. I did not run the code.

CONFIDENCE: 90
